summary.text: A 79-year-old woman with normal pressure hydrocephalus after ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement in the 1980s, nicotine dependence and a 40-year history of meningioma developed sudden right-sided hearing loss four months before her rheumatology clinic presentation. Within one week she had bilateral hearing loss with tinnitus. The otolaryngologist found bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, positive rheumatoid factor and elevated acute phase reactants, and referred her to rheumatology.

Head CT showed a 2.6 cm left frontal lobe meningioma with local mass effect, a ventriculostomy shunt and persistent ventriculomegaly, all stable chronic findings. MRI showed no acute intracranial abnormality and no enhancing retrocochlear mass lesion. At the clinic she had hearing loss, tinnitus, joint pains and brief morning stiffness, took no medication, and the chart showed rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 11 years earlier. Examination, hand X-ray and laboratory results were recorded.

She received smoking cessation counseling and was started on prednisone 60 mg daily. Her hearing impairment significantly improved after four weeks of steroid therapy. Prednisone was gradually tapered and she was started on the steroid-sparing agent/DMARD leflunomide. The abstract reports that her tinnitus resolved completely after treatment with steroids and leflunomide.

ambiguities.issue: The abstract states an unhedged author conclusion that rheumatoid arthritis is the cause of the sensorineural hearing loss, but the case discussion and conclusions hedge it ("could have been most likely", "favors rheumatoid arthritis as the culprit") and name nicotine dependence as a possible contributor. The condition schema has no cause field, and no condition such as rheumatoid arthritis-induced autoimmune inner ear disease is diagnosed for this patient, so the attribution is kept here rather than as a fact.
